Counter 3, dropper corner ring, 8 blocks (track memory): the input cell touches three droppers on three axes (east, up, south); between each pair a hopper carries the stone on to the next dropper (dropper up -> hopper west -> dropper south -> hopper down -> dropper east -> hopper north). Each pulse fires all three; only the one holding the stone moves it, and its hopper delivers it after all three have fired, so the stone advances one dropper per pulse whatever the firing order. The comparator reads the east dropper: on during one pulse window in three (level style).

Counter 2 as a divider, two copper bulbs, 6 blocks (track memory): the input toggles bulb 1, its comparator toggles bulb 2 on every second pulse; bulb 2's comparator changes state once every two pulses and holds between (toggles style). T flip-flop with reset, 8 blocks (track memory): the dropper-ring T flip-flop (two droppers, two hoppers between them, a comparator reading dropper B) with a reset input next to dropper B only. A t pulse fires both droppers (A directly, B through the dust line), only the one holding the stone moves it, and the hoppers hand it to the other dropper after both have fired: q toggles. An r pulse fires B alone: a stone in B leaves (q off at once) and lands in A; with the stone in A nothing moves.

Item counter, 19 items, 39 blocks (track memory, `mctas circuit memory items --n 19`): the one counter whose size does not depend on N. Droppers A and B face each other and hold 19 items between them; each pulse fires exactly one of them, so the pile walks from A to B and back and each dropper runs empty once every 19 pulses. Comparators a and b read them (level 0 only when empty), so the wall torches on their output blocks are lit exactly when their own dropper is empty, and both torches power the copper bulb W above them: W toggles once every 19 pulses and is the output. W is also the phase. Comparator C reads it and its dust line powers the stone south of A, which holds A; the wall torch on that stone is lit only when the line is off, and its line holds B through the stone east of it. A held dropper is one kept continuously powered: it sees no rising edge, so a pulse fires only the other one. The pulse is the dust on the two lids, since a dropper fires on a signal at its own cell or at the cell above it.

Dropper RS latch, 4 blocks (track memory): droppers A (facing east) and B (facing west) face each other and hold one stone. s (next to A) fires A and the stone goes to B; r (next to B) fires B and it comes back; firing the empty one does nothing, so repeated s or r change nothing. A comparator on stone reads B: q is its output (1). Latency 6 gt (dropper 4 + comparator 2). A stack of them tiles with NO gap (`tile: 0 2 0`): a column of latches costs 4 blocks per bit.

Counter 2, one copper bulb, 3 blocks (track memory): the copper bulb T flip-flop seen as a counter: the input toggles the bulb, its comparator's level alternates every pulse (level style, period 2). The same build is tff-bulb, judged as a T flip-flop. A stack of them tiles with NO gap (`tile: 0 2 0`): a counter column costs 3 blocks per stage.

D latch, enable high, with real signal inputs: repeater M carries d to q; subtract comparator C points into M's side with a redstone block at its back, so C gives 15 - e and M is locked while e is off, following d while e is on. The enable arrives on the design's OWN repeater E in the input cell, because a comparator's side never reads a powered plain block: the judge's stone there reads 0.

D flip-flop with enable, 18 blocks: the 15-block repeater-lock flip-flop plus one more lock on the slave. The data runs through two repeaters; the master's lock reads the clock straight (it follows d while the clock is low) and the slave's lock reads it through a wall torch (it passes while the clock is high). The enable gets its own wall torch and repeater, locking the slave from its other side whenever e is off, so a clock edge with e off leaves q alone. Gating the slave instead of the clock needs no AND gate: a repeater is locked if EITHER side is powered.
